sketches.title: Worse Room, Worse Idea
sketches.premise: You are guiding a haunted-house tour, and every move sends the group into one worse room. Say what happens next in the house; the Host hypes it up and roasts any move that gets lazy. Keep making the tour nastier without jumping past the next door.
sketches.criterion: The Judge checks that the move is one new room or room-sized event caused by the whole tour so far, makes the danger or humiliation worse, leaves a clear problem for the next move, and is not a duplicate, a sudden ending, a skipped door, a rewind, a feeling, or a room the house could not contain.
sketches.move_shape: Write up to 140 characters beginning with “Then the tour enters...” and name one connected new room or event; for example: “Then the tour enters a kitchen where the cabinets breathe, and one guest opens the loudest one.”
sketches.first_card: The tour starts in a cheerful coat room; every coat is warm, though nobody is wearing one.

sketches.title: The Host Keeps Lying
sketches.premise: A ghostly host promises that each next room is perfectly safe, while the tour keeps proving the exact opposite. On your turn, add the next lie and the room or stunt that exposes it. Make the host’s sales pitch more desperate, not just the room more gross.
sketches.criterion: The Judge checks that one fresh promise and its immediate contradiction follow from the standing tour, raise the host’s problem, and leave a new lieable detail; a repeated promise, skipped reveal, happy rescue, reversal, unrelated room, or bare insult fails.
sketches.move_shape: Write up to 140 characters as “Then the Host says ___, and the next room shows ___.” Example: “Then the Host says the attic is child-safe, and the floor starts counting the children.”
sketches.first_card: At the welcome desk, the Host smiles and says, “Nothing here can hear you.”

sketches.title: One Bad Request
sketches.premise: The tour group keeps asking the house for small comforts: a drink, a chair, a bathroom, a phone charger. The house grants each request in the worst possible haunted way, and you decide the next request or cruel answer. The joke is watching a normal need become a terrible room.
sketches.criterion: The Judge checks that the move is one new request-and-answer caused by the last need and still inside the house, worsens the group’s practical trouble, and supplies the next need; skipping the request, curing the trouble, ending the tour, undoing a granted item, or adding only a reaction fails.
sketches.move_shape: Write up to 140 characters as “Then someone asks for ___, and the house provides ___.” Example: “Then someone asks for a bathroom, and the nearest door opens onto a toilet that whispers their search history.”
sketches.first_card: A guest asks for water after the first room; the Host points to a clean glass on a silver tray.

sketches.title: Put the Room on Trial
sketches.premise: Each room is accused of one crime against the tour, and the next room must present evidence, a witness, or a punishment. You are building a crooked trial as the group moves deeper into the house. The Host gives savage commentary whenever a room’s case is flimsy.
sketches.criterion: The Judge checks that the move adds one concrete piece of trial business caused by the current accusation and moves the case toward a worse ruling, while keeping the tour in the next room; a verdict without evidence, a skipped hearing step, acquittal, undo, duplicate claim, or pure opinion fails.
sketches.move_shape: Write up to 140 characters as “Then the next room presents ___ as evidence against ___.” Example: “Then the pantry presents 400 labeled teeth as evidence that the kitchen eats guests.”
sketches.first_card: The foyer is accused of hiding the exit; its only evidence is a welcome mat that points in three directions.

sketches.title: Who Gets Sent First
sketches.premise: The haunted house keeps forcing the tour group to choose who goes first, who stays behind, or who holds the awful object. Each move makes one group choice, then shows the immediate consequence in the next room. Be cruel to the situation, not vague: the house must use the choice.
sketches.criterion: The Judge checks that the move makes one forced group choice caused by the last threat and shows its immediate new consequence, increasing the danger or unfairness; a choice with no result, a leap to the disaster’s aftermath, a rescue, a reversal, a duplicate choice, or a feeling alone fails.
sketches.move_shape: Write up to 140 characters as “Then the group sends ___ first, so ___ happens in the next room.” Example: “Then the group sends the tallest guest first, so the ceiling lowers to exactly their height.”
sketches.first_card: A locked door asks for one volunteer to carry the ringing brass bell; the group has not chosen yet.

sketches.title: New Rule, Worse House
sketches.premise: The house reveals one rule at a time, and the tour must obey each rule while discovering why it exists. On your turn, add the next plain rule and the immediate room event that proves it is awful. The goal is a growing rulebook nobody should have signed.
sketches.criterion: The Judge checks that one new rule and its first proof follow from the standing rules and room, make later movement harder, and leave a usable detail for the next rule; a rule with no proof, a skipped first violation, an escape, a rule that cancels another, a duplicate, or a moral fails.
sketches.move_shape: Write up to 140 characters as “Then the house reveals: ‘___’; the next room proves it when ___.” Example: “Then the house reveals: ‘Never look up’; the next room’s key hangs from a face in the ceiling.”
sketches.first_card: At the first door, a brass plate reads: “Rule one: Do not thank the house.”
